reading5.title: The Cemetery Drawer
reading5.text:
For most of my twenties I kept a drawer that I referred to, with what I imagined was wry self-awareness, as the cemetery. Into it went the openings of novels — never more than forty pages, often far fewer — that had seemed, for a week or a month, to be the book I was born to write. I would buy a new notebook for each one, as though the stationery itself might confer commitment, and I would abandon each one at roughly the same point: the moment the characters stopped doing what I had planned and began, in some faint but unmistakable way, to want things of their own.

I did not understand then that this was the moment the work was beginning rather than ending. I took the resistance as evidence of failure, a sign that I had misjudged the material or, worse, that I lacked whatever quality separated real writers from people who merely liked the idea of being one. My father, a carpenter who had never read a novel he did not consider too long, offered the only advice I remember from that period. “Wood argues back,” he told me once, watching his daughter glare at a notebook on the kitchen table. “That's how you know it's wood.” I nodded politely and assumed he was talking about wood.

The drawer grew. By the time I was twenty-eight it held eleven beginnings, and I had begun to suspect that the count itself was the point — that I was less a novelist than a collector of first chapters, someone who loved the clean, unearned optimism of page one and could not bear what came after. Friends who wrote were kind about this in the way people are kind about a relative's unusual diet: interested, slightly wary, careful never to suggest an alternative.

What changed was not discipline, or not at first. It was a flood. A pipe burst in the apartment upstairs one February while I was away, and I came home to find the ceiling of my study sagging like a wet sail and the drawer, which sat directly beneath the worst of it, swollen shut. When I finally pried it open, most of the notebooks had fused into a single grey brick. Only one had survived more or less intact, protected by the others piled on top of it: the most recent and, in many ways, the least promising, a story about a woman who repairs clocks in a town that has stopped caring what time it is.

I would love to report that I saw the hand of fate in this. In truth I was mostly annoyed, and a little relieved, the way one is relieved when a decision one has been avoiding is made by the weather. But the relief turned out to matter. With the cemetery gone, there was nowhere to bury the clock book when it began, as they all did, to argue back. I could abandon it, certainly, but I would have to do so in the open, with no drawer to receive it and no comforting sense that it was joining a distinguished company of the almost.

So I kept going, largely out of a reluctance to start a twelfth notebook. The woman who repaired clocks became difficult, then interesting, then someone I could not predict. She refused the romance I had planned for her and devoted herself instead to an elderly neighbour's bad-tempered parrot, a development I resisted for three months and have never since regretted. The book took four years. It is not a great novel, but it is a finished one, and I have come to think that the distance between those two things is smaller than the distance between a finished novel and a drawer full of brilliant openings.

I still think about my father's remark, though I understand it differently now. He was not offering encouragement, exactly. He was describing a property of material that anyone who works with their hands learns early and writers often learn late: that resistance is not a verdict on the maker but a sign that there is something real on the bench.

questions.q: In the first paragraph, the phrase “with what I imagined was wry self-awareness” suggests that the writer now
choices: considers the drawer to have been a useful part of her creative process.
feels that the name she gave the drawer was unfairly harsh.
regrets having joked about work that had cost her so much effort.
doubts that she understood her habit as clearly as she believed at the time.
questions.explain: « What I imagined » montre qu'elle se croyait lucide et ironique à l'époque ; avec le recul, elle doute de cette lucidité, puisqu'elle n'avait pas compris le vrai problème (paragraphe 2).

questions.q: According to the second paragraph, what did the writer fail to understand at the time?
choices: that her father's remark was intended as a criticism of her habits
that other writers she knew had experienced the same difficulty
that her material would have suited a different literary form
that characters resisting her plans marked the real start of the work
questions.explain: Elle écrit « this was the moment the work was beginning rather than ending » : quand les personnages lui échappaient, le vrai travail commençait ; elle y voyait à tort un échec.

questions.q: The comparison with “a relative's unusual diet” in the third paragraph conveys her friends'
choices: tactful unwillingness to challenge her way of working.
open disapproval of the time she was wasting.
lack of interest in what she was writing.
envy of the freedom she seemed to enjoy.
questions.explain: Les amis sont « interested, slightly wary, careful never to suggest an alternative » : polis, un peu inquiets, ils évitent de la contredire ; ils ne sont ni désapprobateurs ni indifférents.

questions.q: How did the writer react when she discovered the damage caused by the flood?
choices: She took it as a sign that she was destined to finish the surviving story.
She was devastated by the loss of what she considered her best ideas.
She felt partly released from a decision she had been putting off.
She resolved to rewrite the lost beginnings from memory.
questions.explain: Elle était « mostly annoyed, and a little relieved », comme quand la météo tranche une décision qu'on repoussait ; elle rejette explicitement l'idée du destin (« I would love to report that I saw the hand of fate »).

questions.q: In the fifth paragraph, “a distinguished company of the almost” refers to
choices: writers she admired who had never completed a book.
the abandoned openings she had previously stored away.
the characters who had escaped her original plans.
the friends who had read her unfinished work.
questions.explain: Le roman de l'horlogère aurait « rejoint » les débuts de romans abandonnés dans le tiroir : « the almost » désigne ironiquement ces projets presque aboutis.

questions.q: What point does the writer make in the final paragraph?
choices: Difficulty in a piece of work is a sign that it has genuine substance.
Her father had always secretly believed in her talent.
Writers should acquire a practical craft before attempting fiction.
People who work with their hands are generally wiser than writers.
questions.explain: La résistance n'est « pas un verdict sur l'artisan » mais le signe qu'il y a « something real on the bench » ; elle précise d'ailleurs que son père ne cherchait pas vraiment à l'encourager.

reading5.title: The Mind Without a Brain
reading5.text:
Somewhere in a laboratory, a yellow blob is solving a problem. It has no eyes, no nerves and nothing that could reasonably be called a head, yet over the course of a few hours it will find its way to food by a route that a human engineer, given a map and a pencil, might struggle to improve upon. The blob is a slime mould, and for the past couple of decades it has been quietly embarrassing some of our most cherished assumptions about what it takes to be clever.

The species most often studied, known to researchers by its Latin name, Physarum polycephalum, is not a fungus, despite its appearance and its habit of turning up on rotting logs. Nor is it a plant or an animal. For much of its life it exists as a single enormous cell containing a vast number of nuclei, a pulsing network of tubes through which its contents flow back and forth in rhythmic waves. When it detects something it wants — oat flakes are a laboratory favourite — the tubes leading towards the food thicken, and those leading nowhere gradually wither away.

It was this simple rule of reinforcement that first caught the attention of scientists. Researchers in Japan placed the mould at the entrance to a small maze and food at the exit; the organism, having initially spread itself through every corridor, retracted from the dead ends until only the shortest path remained. In a later experiment, oat flakes were arranged in the pattern of the cities surrounding Tokyo, and the mould wove a network between them that bore a striking resemblance to the region's actual railway system — a system that had taken teams of planners many years to design.

It is tempting, at this point, to reach for the word “intelligent”, and many headlines have done so with enthusiasm. Yet the scientists involved tend to be more cautious, and with reason. Nothing in the mould's behaviour requires us to imagine that it knows what a maze is, or that it is, in any meaningful sense, trying. What it is doing is following local rules — grow towards this, retreat from that — whose cumulative effect happens to look, from where we stand, remarkably like a decision. The cleverness, one might argue, is in the eye of the beholder.

And yet that argument, pushed far enough, begins to cut in uncomfortable directions. Our own neurons, after all, are also following local rules; no single cell in the human brain understands chess, or grief, or the plot of a novel. If we decide that the slime mould is merely mechanical because its problem-solving emerges from simple interactions, we may find ourselves obliged to say something similar about ourselves. The difference between us may be one of scale and complexity rather than of kind — a conclusion that some find thrilling and others faintly insulting.

There are further puzzles. As it explores, the mould leaves behind a trail of slime that it subsequently avoids, so that it does not waste energy searching the same ground twice. Some researchers have described this as a kind of external memory: rather than storing information inside itself, the organism writes it onto the world. Humans, of course, do much the same thing with shopping lists, calendars and notes stuck to the fridge, and few of us would claim that our memory is any less ours for being partly kept on paper.

None of this means that we should start consulting slime moulds about transit policy, although the idea of borrowing their methods to design networks has been taken surprisingly seriously. What the blob offers is less a model to copy than a mirror to look into. It invites us to consider whether intelligence is something an organism possesses or a pattern that emerges whenever living matter meets a problem — and whether the line we draw between thinking and merely behaving was ever quite as firm as we supposed.

questions.q: In the first paragraph, the writer suggests that slime moulds have
choices: unsettled long-held ideas about what problem-solving requires.
consistently outperformed human planners in design tasks.
been studied mainly by engineers rather than biologists.
only recently been discovered by researchers.
questions.explain: « Quietly embarrassing some of our most cherished assumptions about what it takes to be clever » : elles bousculent nos idées sur l'intelligence. Le texte dit seulement qu'un ingénieur « might struggle to improve upon » leur trajet, pas qu'elles le battent toujours.

questions.q: The writer mentions the railway system around Tokyo in order to emphasize
choices: how easily the experiment could be repeated in other cities.
that the mould produced, without any plan, what humans had needed years to design.
that the design of the real network had been influenced by the mould.
that the mould's network was more efficient than the real one.
questions.explain: La précision « a system that had taken teams of planners many years to design » souligne le contraste entre l'effort humain et le résultat obtenu par la moisissure ; on parle de ressemblance, pas de supériorité.

questions.q: What is the writer's attitude in the fourth paragraph towards headlines calling the mould “intelligent”?
choices: They accurately reflect the scientists' own conclusions.
They underestimate what the mould is capable of.
They were deliberately designed to mislead readers.
They overlook the possibility that simple rules explain the behaviour.
questions.explain: L'auteur oppose l'enthousiasme des titres à la prudence des chercheurs : le comportement s'explique peut-être par de simples « local rules », sans intention. Rien n'indique une volonté de tromper.

questions.q: What does the writer mean by saying that the argument begins to “cut in uncomfortable directions”?
choices: The reasoning used to deny the mould intelligence could equally be applied to humans.
Scientists studying the mould have begun to disagree with one another.
Research on neurons has proved harder than research on moulds.
The mould's abilities have turned out to be greater than first thought.
questions.explain: Nos neurones suivent eux aussi des règles locales : si la moisissure n'est qu'un mécanisme, il faudrait en dire autant de nous, d'où le malaise.

questions.q: The writer refers to shopping lists and calendars in order to
choices: show that human memory is less reliable than we believe.
argue that the mould's memory is more efficient than ours.
suggest that storing information outside oneself does not make it any less a form of memory.
highlight a fundamental difference between humans and moulds.
questions.explain: « Few of us would claim that our memory is any less ours for being partly kept on paper » : c'est un parallèle qui légitime l'idée de mémoire externe chez la moisissure, pas une différence.

questions.q: In the final paragraph, the writer concludes that the slime mould is valuable chiefly because it
choices: provides engineers with a practical model for transport networks.
prompts us to question where the boundary between thinking and behaving lies.
proves that intelligence does not require a brain.
shows that human intelligence has been overestimated.
questions.explain: La moisissure est « less a model to copy than a mirror » : elle nous oblige à nous demander si la frontière entre penser et simplement agir est aussi nette qu'on le croyait ; l'auteur ne prétend rien « prouver ».

reading5.title: In Praise of the Bad Recommendation
reading5.text:
There is a particular kind of disappointment that has almost vanished from modern life, and I find, somewhat to my surprise, that I miss it. It is the disappointment of the bad recommendation: the novel a well-meaning aunt pressed upon you at a family dinner, the film a friend insisted you would adore, the album bought on the strength of an intriguing cover that turned out to contain forty minutes of something you could barely endure. These were small failures, but they were failures with faces attached, and they taught us something that the smooth machinery of personalized suggestion seems determined to spare us.

I should make clear that I am not about to mourn the passing of some golden age. The old ways of discovering culture were inefficient, frequently snobbish and heavily dependent on accidents of geography and income. If you grew up, as I did, in a small town with one bookshop whose owner regarded science fiction as a moral failing, your options were limited in ways that no amount of nostalgia can make charming. The systems that now suggest what we might read, watch or listen to next have opened doors that were firmly shut to previous generations, and anyone who dismisses them wholesale is, I suspect, speaking from a position of considerable privilege.

And yet. The promise of these systems is that they know us — or rather, that they know the version of us that can be inferred from what we have already chosen. This is a subtle but significant distinction. A recommendation built on past behaviour is, by its nature, a bet that we will continue to be who we have been. It is extraordinarily good at offering more of the same, slightly varied, and correspondingly poor at offering the thing we did not know we wanted because we had not yet become the person who would want it.

The aunt with the novel was not, of course, working from a data set. She was working from a hunch, an affection and, quite often, a profound misreading of her niece's tastes. But her misreading was itself informative. It told me how I appeared to someone who loved me, which was not always how I appeared to myself, and on more than one occasion the book I had expected to loathe turned out to be the one I needed. Even the failures carried a kind of information: in working out precisely why I disliked something, I came to understand what I valued.

It would be easy to conclude from all this that we should switch off the machines and return to browsing dusty shelves. That is not my argument, and it would be a futile one in any case. What I am suggesting is something more modest: that we cultivate, deliberately, a tolerance for the poorly matched. Ask the people around you what they are reading and then read it, especially if it sounds unpromising. Accept the friend's invitation to the concert you would never have chosen. Treat the occasional wasted evening not as a malfunction but as the price of remaining capable of surprise.

There is a broader point here about what we expect culture to do for us. If a novel or a film is simply a product designed to satisfy existing preferences, then a system that predicts those preferences flawlessly is the ideal guide. But the works that matter most to us rarely feel, at first, like satisfaction. They feel like interruption — an argument we were not expecting, a voice we had to learn to hear. A culture organized entirely around what we already like risks becoming very comfortable and very small.

My aunt, incidentally, still sends me books. Most of them are not to my taste. I read every one.

questions.q: What does the writer mean by describing bad recommendations as “failures with faces attached”?
choices: They came from people one knew personally.
They damaged the reputations of the critics who made them.
They made the writer resent the friends who offered them.
They were usually based on misleading cover images.
questions.explain: Les mauvais conseils venaient d'une tante, d'un ami : des personnes réelles et proches, contrairement aux suggestions anonymes des algorithmes.

questions.q: In the second paragraph, the writer is concerned to
choices: argue that cultural life was richer in small towns.
criticize people who depend on technology for their choices.
acknowledge the genuine advantages of modern recommendation systems.
explain how a bookshop owner shaped her reading habits.
questions.explain: Elle refuse la nostalgie (« I am not about to mourn the passing of some golden age ») et reconnaît que ces systèmes « have opened doors » ; la librairie n'est qu'un exemple des limites d'autrefois.

questions.q: The “subtle but significant distinction” in the third paragraph is between
choices: suggestions made by people and those made by machines.
who we are and who our past choices suggest we are.
entertainment we enjoy and culture we need.
variety and repetition in what is recommended.
questions.explain: « They know us — or rather, … the version of us that can be inferred from what we have already chosen » : la nuance oppose notre personne réelle à l'image déduite de nos choix passés.

questions.q: What does the writer value about her aunt's recommendations?
choices: They were usually more accurate than she had expected.
They were based on a detailed knowledge of her reading.
They introduced her to authors her aunt had loved as a child.
They revealed how others saw her and helped her define her own tastes.
questions.explain: L'erreur de la tante lui montrait comment la voyait une personne aimante, et comprendre pourquoi elle n'aimait pas un livre l'aidait à savoir ce qu'elle valorisait ; ces conseils étaient souvent à côté de la plaque.

questions.q: The writer's proposal in the fifth paragraph is best described as
choices: a modest change in personal habits rather than a rejection of technology.
a call to abandon digital services in favour of bookshops.
a plan for making recommendation systems less predictable.
an admission that wasted evenings can never be avoided.
questions.explain: « That is not my argument… What I am suggesting is something more modest » : cultiver soi-même une tolérance pour les choix mal assortis, sans éteindre les machines.

questions.q: What does the final paragraph suggest about the writer?
choices: She has come to share her aunt's taste in books.
She regrets not having been more honest with her aunt.
She has persuaded her aunt to send fewer books.
She acts on the advice she gives in the essay.
questions.explain: Elle lit tous les livres reçus alors qu'ils ne sont pas à son goût : elle pratique la « tolerance for the poorly matched » qu'elle recommande.

reading5.title: The Singing Lake
reading5.text:
I had been warned about the noise, but warnings, I have since learned, are a poor preparation for most things worth experiencing. We were perhaps a hundred metres from the shore when the first sound came up through the ice beneath us — a long, descending note, somewhere between the call of a whale and the whine of a stone skimming across a frozen pond, that seemed to travel away from us towards the far side of the lake and then, unaccountably, return. I stopped walking. Marguerite, who had been leading the way with the unhurried confidence of someone crossing her own kitchen, did not.

“It does that,” she called over her shoulder. “It means it's thick.”

This was, I would come to understand, entirely characteristic. Marguerite had taught science at the local school for the better part of thirty years and had a teacher's fondness for explanation, but she rationed it carefully, as though aware that understanding something too quickly might spoil it. She had agreed to take me onto the lake on the condition, stated firmly over the phone, that I would not try to “make it into a story”. I had agreed, and was already, as we both knew, breaking my word.

The science, when she eventually offered it, was straightforward enough. Ice expands and contracts as temperatures shift, and on a large lake the resulting stresses are released in cracks that can run for considerable distances. Because the ice behaves something like the skin of a drum, the sound of each fracture is carried far and strangely distorted, the higher frequencies arriving before the lower ones, so that a single crack is heard as a sweeping, otherworldly whistle. None of this, she pointed out, indicated danger. A lake that sings is a lake that is solid enough to carry the song.

I would like to say that this reassured me. It did, intellectually. But there is a part of the mind that does not attend lectures, and that part spent the next hour convinced that every note was the overture to catastrophe. I walked as though the ice were a sleeping animal I did not wish to wake, placing my feet with exaggerated care and flinching at each new sound, while Marguerite strode ahead and occasionally stopped to point out things I was too preoccupied to see: the tracks of a fox that had crossed during the night, a cluster of bubbles hanging in the ice like a frozen constellation, the precise blue of the light where the wind had swept the snow away.

It was somewhere in the middle of the lake, with the shore reduced to a dark line of spruce on every side, that something shifted. I could not tell you exactly when. The sounds had not stopped — if anything, they had grown more frequent as the afternoon cooled — but I had stopped hearing them as warnings. They had become, instead, a kind of conversation going on beneath us, one in which we were not participants but were, it seemed, tolerated. I found that I was walking normally. I found, absurdly, that I was listening for the next one.

On the way back, I asked Marguerite whether she ever grew tired of the sound. She considered the question for longer than I expected. “No,” she said finally. “But I've stopped trying to describe it to people. They either come out here or they don't.” Then she glanced at my notebook, and at me, and very nearly smiled.

questions.q: What does the writer suggest about the warnings received before the walk?
choices: They had exaggerated the danger of crossing the ice.
They could not convey what the experience was really like.
They had been given by Marguerite over the phone.
They had been deliberately ignored.
questions.explain: « Warnings … are a poor preparation for most things worth experiencing » : être prévenu ne prépare pas vraiment à ce qu'on vit ; rien ne dit que le danger était exagéré.

questions.q: What is implied by the phrase “as we both knew” in the third paragraph?
choices: Marguerite had already changed her mind about her condition.
The writer had told Marguerite about a planned article.
Both of them had doubts about whether the trip was wise.
Marguerite was aware that the writer would inevitably turn the walk into a story.
questions.explain: Le narrateur avait promis de ne pas « make it into a story » et rompt déjà sa promesse ; « as we both knew » montre que Marguerite n'était pas dupe (d'où le carnet à la fin).

questions.q: According to the fourth paragraph, the sounds made by the ice
choices: are caused by water moving beneath the surface.
show that the ice is strong enough to walk on.
warn that a large crack is about to open.
grow louder as the weather becomes warmer.
questions.explain: « A lake that sings is a lake that is solid enough to carry the song » : le bruit, produit par des fissures, prouve l'épaisseur de la glace et n'annonce aucun danger.

questions.q: In the fifth paragraph, “a part of the mind that does not attend lectures” refers to
choices: an instinctive fear that rational explanation cannot reach.
the writer's difficulty in concentrating on Marguerite's words.
unpleasant memories of school science lessons.
a curiosity that prefers experience to theory.
questions.explain: Le narrateur est rassuré « intellectually », mais une partie instinctive de lui reste terrifiée : l'explication scientifique (la « lecture ») ne l'atteint pas.

questions.q: What change is described in the sixth paragraph?
choices: The writer finally caught up with Marguerite.
The sounds of the ice became less frequent.
The writer stopped hearing the sounds as a threat.
The writer began to understand the science of the ice.
questions.explain: « I had stopped hearing them as warnings » : les sons deviennent une « conversation » ; ils sont même plus fréquents, et la science avait déjà été expliquée avant.

questions.q: What does Marguerite's answer in the final paragraph suggest about her?
choices: She believes the experience can only truly be understood at first hand.
She has grown tired of the sound after so many years.
She regrets having agreed to take the writer onto the lake.
She thinks most visitors are too nervous to enjoy the lake.
questions.explain: « They either come out here or they don't » : pour elle, les mots ne suffisent pas, il faut venir sur la glace ; et elle répond « No » à la question de la lassitude.

reading6.title: Late Strings
parts: When I told my family that I intended, at the age of forty-five, to learn the cello, the reaction was broadly supportive in the way that reactions to midlife announcements tend to be: warm, encouraging and laced with a faint, unspoken expectation that the enthusiasm would pass by spring. My daughter, who had abandoned the clarinet at eleven, asked whether I knew how big a cello was. I said I did. I did not.
{gap}

Getting it home was, however, the easy part. My first teacher, a brisk retired orchestral player named Hélène, took one look at the way I was holding the bow and asked, not unkindly, whether I had ever held anything at all. She then spent the entire first lesson on that question alone, without allowing me to play a single note.
{gap}

Tension, it turned out, was going to be my principal adversary. Adults, Hélène explained, bring to an instrument not only their enthusiasm but every habit their bodies have accumulated over decades of sitting at desks, carrying groceries and bracing themselves against the world. Children, by contrast, arrive more or less unfurnished.
{gap}

That place, she said, was pride. We adults were used to being competent. We had careers, opinions and mortgages, and we found it almost unbearable to sound, week after week, like a door being opened very slowly in an old house. Many of her adult students, she told me, gave up not because they lacked ability but because they could not tolerate the sound of their own beginnings.
{gap}

There was no single reason. Work became busier; a cold lingered for weeks; the spare room was needed for a visiting relative. Each interruption was reasonable in itself, but together they produced a silence that grew harder to break the longer it lasted. The cello stood in its corner, accusing me in the way that only large, expensive objects can.
{gap}

The piece we settled on was short, slow and, by any objective standard, very easy. I practised it with a desperation I had not felt since my school exams, and on the evening of the concert I played it to an audience of perhaps thirty people, most of them relatives of children who played far better than I did.
{gap}

I have thought about that man often since. I never learned his name, and I do not know whether he ever bought his violin. But his remark crystallized something Hélène had been trying to tell me from the very first lesson: that the point of playing badly in public is not to be admired, but to give other people permission.
{gap}

Not everyone takes the advice, and I have learned not to press it. Occasionally, though, it is taken by someone I never addressed at all. My daughter, I recently discovered, has quietly dug her old clarinet out of the basement. She has not mentioned it, and neither, wisely, have I.
options: I resolved not to be one of them, and for a while my resolve held. I practised every evening after dinner, in the spare room with the door firmly closed, and kept a notebook in which I recorded, with the rigour of a laboratory scientist, the number of minutes spent on each exercise. Then, in the middle of my second winter, I stopped.

I found out on the morning I collected the rented instrument from a shop on the other side of town. It came in a case roughly the size and shape of a small canoe, and getting it into the car required the folding of seats, the removal of a booster seat and a degree of geometrical improvisation I had not attempted since university.

Hélène's own career had begun much earlier. She had been placed in front of a cello at the age of four by a mother who believed that every child should play something, and she had performed with orchestras across the country before moving to our city to be nearer her grandchildren.

I made two mistakes that I noticed and, I am reliably informed, several that I did not. Nobody seemed to mind. Afterwards, an elderly man came up to tell me that he had wanted to learn the violin for most of his life, and that watching me had persuaded him it might not be too late. I have rarely received a compliment I deserved less or valued more.

At the time, this struck me as excessive, even faintly theatrical. I had paid for music, after all, and was receiving instead a lecture on the weight of my own arm. It was only months later, listening to recordings of myself, that I understood what she had been protecting me from: a lifetime of tension that, once learned, would have taken far longer to undo than to acquire.

It is a permission I have since tried to extend to others. When colleagues confess, as they often do, to some long-abandoned ambition — the piano, a language, painting — I no longer simply nod sympathetically. I tell them about the canoe-shaped case, the lesson without notes and the man who wanted a violin, and I suggest, as gently as I can, that they start before spring.

That is not to say that children have it easy. Hélène taught several, and she was candid about the ways in which they struggled: short attention spans, small hands, parents with unrealistic timetables. But she was equally candid that the adult learner's chief difficulty lay elsewhere, in a place no amount of stretching could reach.

What finally brought me back was not discipline but embarrassment. Hélène, whom I had been avoiding with a series of increasingly creative excuses, telephoned one evening to say that she was organizing a small concert for her students and had already put my name on the program. I opened my mouth to refuse, and heard myself ask what I should play.
reading6.explain: Indices : « I did not » → « I found out » (B) ; « that question alone… without a single note » → « this struck me as excessive » (E), qui finit sur « tension », repris par « Tension, it turned out » ; « Children… unfurnished » → « not to say that children have it easy… a place » (G) → « That place… was pride » ; « gave up » → « not to be one of them… I stopped » (A) → « There was no single reason » ; le silence → « What finally brought me back » (H) → « The piece we settled on » ; le concert → les erreurs et « an elderly man » (D) → « that man » ; « permission » → « It is a permission » (F) → « Not everyone takes the advice ». C (carrière d'Hélène) est l'intrus : aucun paragraphe ne reprend ses idées.

reading6.title: While the City Sleeps
parts: At eleven o'clock on a weeknight, when most of the street has drawn its curtains, the lights come on at the back of a small bakery near the river. Inside, Nadia Okafor ties on an apron that has clearly seen better decades, switches on a radio permanently tuned to a classical station, and begins the first of the night's many negotiations with flour, water and time.
{gap}

This means that her working day, if it can be called that, runs in overlapping loops rather than a straight line. At any given moment she is finishing something begun hours ago while preparing something that will not be finished until tomorrow. Visitors, she says, find this disorienting. She finds it the only sensible way to live.
{gap}

Nadia laughs at the memory, but she is sympathetic. It took her, she admits, the better part of two years to adjust to working through the night when she first took over the bakery from its previous owner, a man who had run it for most of his adult life and who stayed on for six months to teach her his methods.
{gap}

She did, in a few respects. Orders are now taken online, and the ancient oven, which had a habit of breaking down on public holidays, has been replaced. But on the question of the bread itself, she found herself, to her own surprise, siding with the old man. The shortcuts she had planned would have saved hours, but the loaves they produced tasted, as she puts it, of nothing in particular.
{gap}

That baguette, Nadia says, was the most useful piece of market research she has ever received. She returned to the slower method the following week and has not wavered since. Business has grown steadily, largely by word of mouth, and these days a modest queue forms on the sidewalk most mornings before the doors open.
{gap}

The stillness does not last. By four the ovens are full and the kitchen has become a place of heat, noise and rapid decisions, with trays emerging and disappearing in a rhythm that leaves no room for conversation. This is the part of the job that most resembles the frantic image people have of professional kitchens, and it is, Nadia insists, the least interesting.
{gap}

These small variations are, she says, the whole point. Flour changes from one delivery to the next; humidity rises and falls with the weather; even her own mood, she suspects, finds its way into the dough. A baker who expects identical results every night will be perpetually disappointed. One who accepts the variations, and learns from them, will never be bored.
{gap}
She will be back, of course, by eleven. The sourdough for tomorrow is already waiting.
options: Those methods were, by modern standards, almost perversely laborious. He weighed everything by hand, refused to use the ready-made yeast blends on which most bakeries rely, and insisted that every loaf be shaped individually rather than by machine. Nadia's first instinct, as a business graduate with a spreadsheet for every occasion, was to modernize.

The previous owner, she later learned, had himself trained in a bakery in Lyon, where he had worked nights for nearly a decade before emigrating. He rarely spoke about those years, but he kept a faded photograph of the shop pinned above the sink, and it hangs there still.

What interests her more is what happens afterwards, in the quiet hour between the last tray and the first customer. This is when she tastes, adjusts and takes notes, comparing tonight's loaves with last week's and trying to understand why a particular batch has turned out a fraction denser or a shade paler than she intended.

Time is the ingredient she talks about most. Bread, she explains, cannot be hurried without paying for it later in flavour and texture, and much of her craft consists of arranging the night so that each dough is ready precisely when she is. The sourdough she shapes tonight was started yesterday afternoon; the croissants that will be sold at seven were prepared before she went home to sleep.

Long before that queue begins to form, however, there is a stretch of the night that Nadia describes as her favourite. Somewhere around three o'clock, with the first batches rising and nothing yet ready for the oven, the bakery falls into a kind of suspended stillness. She makes herself a coffee, sits on an upturned crate by the back door and listens to the city doing nothing at all.

Bored she certainly is not. At seven, when she unlocks the front door and the first customers come in out of the cold, she greets most of them by name and asks after their families, as if she had not already been awake and working for eight hours. Only when the morning rush has subsided does she hand over to her day staff, hang up the apron and go home to sleep.

One such visitor was her nephew, who spent a week of his summer vacation working alongside her and lasted, by her account, until the third night. He was willing and strong, she says, but he kept asking what time it was, as if the answer might change something.

Customers noticed, too. During a brief experiment with a faster recipe in her first winter, several regulars came in to ask, with the tact of people who have bought the same loaf for twenty years, whether everything was all right. One elderly woman simply handed back a half-eaten baguette and walked out without a word.

reading6.title: The Rivers Beneath Our Feet
parts: The first clue, Theo Marchetti tells me, is usually a dip in the road. Not a pothole or a sag caused by careless resurfacing, but a long, gentle depression that runs across a street at an angle no planner would have chosen, as if the asphalt were remembering something. Once you learn to see them, he says, you notice them everywhere.
{gap}

Theo, a retired land surveyor, is one of about a dozen members of an informal group that has spent the past several years trying to map these lost waterways. They meet on the first Sunday of every month, armed with old maps, a few borrowed instruments and an enthusiasm that their families regard with amused patience.
{gap}

To close the gap between the map and the ground, the group turns to the city itself. Besides dips in the road, they look for clusters of damp basements, unexpectedly lush strips of grass in otherwise parched parks, and buildings whose foundations have shifted in a telltale line. Street names help too: more than one avenue in the city still bears the name of a brook that vanished long before anyone now living was born.
{gap}

Goosebumps aside, the group is careful about what it claims. Members record their findings on a shared online map, marking each section of stream with a line that reflects their confidence: solid where the route has been confirmed by city records, dotted where it remains educated speculation. Theo is fond of pointing out that the dotted lines vastly outnumber the solid ones.
{gap}

That episode, Theo says, changed how the group thinks about its work. What had begun as a pastime — a way of getting retired surveyors and curious neighbours out of the house — suddenly seemed to have practical consequences. Several members began reading about flood management, and the group has since been invited to share its map with a committee studying the city's aging drainage network.
{gap}

Theo understands the concern, but does not share it. For him, the pleasure and the usefulness have always been connected. Knowing that a stream runs beneath a particular street changes the way you walk down it, he argues; you begin to understand the city as something layered and alive, shaped by forces older than any of its buildings.
{gap}

Theo is realistic about the prospects of anything similar happening here. The costs are considerable, and most of the city's lost streams now run beneath land far too valuable to dig up. But he does not rule it out entirely. Cities change, he points out, and the streams have been patient.
{gap}
As we part, Theo hands me a photocopy of an old map with a thin blue line running through my own neighbourhood. I have not yet gone looking. I suspect, though, that I will.
options: Not everyone welcomes the new seriousness. One founding member, a former schoolteacher, worries that the group risks losing the spirit of play that drew her to it in the first place. She joined, she says, because she loved the idea of a secret geography hidden in plain sight, not to attend meetings about infrastructure.

The old maps are the starting point. Before the streams disappeared, surveyors recorded them with considerable care, and by laying these historical documents over modern street plans, the group can estimate where a stream once ran. But the estimates are rarely precise. Early maps were drawn by hand, often at small scales, and a line that looks confident on paper may represent little more than a guess.

In the meantime, the group continues its monthly walks. On the Sunday I join them, we spend three hours tracing a single stream across a dozen blocks, losing it twice and finding it again thanks to the faint dampness of a hedge and a dip in the road that, now that I know what to look for, I cannot stop seeing.

Theo first became interested in the subject as a child, when his family's basement flooded every spring for reasons no plumber could explain. Years later, examining an old map at work, he noticed a stream marked directly beneath his childhood street, and the mystery was finally solved.

What the asphalt remembers, more often than not, is water. Like many older cities, this one was built across a landscape threaded with streams, and as the streets spread outwards, most of those streams were diverted into pipes and buried. Today they still flow, unseen, beneath parking lots, schoolyards and the basements of houses whose owners have no idea they are there.

This caution has earned the group a degree of respect that its members did not expect. Last year, a planner from the city's engineering department contacted them after a stretch of new road began to subside, asking whether they had any information about the area. They did. The dotted line on their map, it turned out, ran almost exactly beneath the damage.

That understanding has inspired more ambitious projects elsewhere. In a number of cities around the world, buried streams have been brought back to the surface, a process sometimes known as daylighting, and turned into parks and walkways that cool the surrounding streets and give wildlife a foothold in the urban landscape.

Occasionally the evidence is more direct. On quiet evenings, standing over certain storm drains, members swear that they can hear the buried water running far below — a faint, steady rush quite unlike the gurgle of an ordinary drain after rain. Theo admits that this is not the most scientific of methods. “But it's the one that gives you goosebumps,” he says.

reading7.title: Counting for Science: four volunteers on citizen science

sections.label: A
sections.text: Eleanor, winter bird count. I would never have signed up on my own. When I retired, a neighbour who coordinates the count for our district more or less appeared on my doorstep with a clipboard and informed me that I had a garden, a window and, now, no excuse. What I had not anticipated was how little I had actually been looking. I had shared my garden with chickadees and juncos for twenty years and could not have told you, with any confidence, how many visited on a given morning or how they behaved towards one another. Counting forces a kind of attention that casual enjoyment never does. The work is not always cheerful: over the past few winters the evening grosbeaks that once descended on our feeders in noisy crowds have dwindled to the odd pair, and recording that decline, year after year, has been a quietly melancholy business. But at least it is now written down somewhere it might matter.

sections.label: B
sections.text: Raj, galaxy classification. I came to it through insomnia. Rather than lie awake, I started browsing online projects and found one that asks volunteers to sort telescope images of galaxies by shape. My first reaction was something close to panic: who was I to be making judgments that astronomers would rely on? I was convinced I would introduce some catastrophic error into the research. It was a relief to discover that every image is shown to many volunteers, and that the system is designed to absorb the occasional wrong answer. Since then the main problem has been the opposite one. There is always one more image, and I have more than once looked up to find that it is getting light outside. I have also been struck by the project's discussion forum, where professional researchers answer the most naive questions with a patience and good humour I had not expected from people so obviously busy.

sections.label: C
sections.text: Marisol, river water testing. The idea was mine. I wanted a summer project that would get my two teenagers away from their screens, and testing the river behind our town seemed educational without being obviously so. The kits are simple: a few vials, some colour charts and a notebook. My son lost interest within two weeks and rejoined, rather sheepishly, when his sister's results started to look interesting. In August our readings showed bacteria levels well above the safe limit near the public beach, and after the municipality ran its own tests, the beach was closed for ten days. Seeing a sign go up because of numbers we had written down at the kitchen table was extraordinary. What I found harder to accept was the reaction of a couple of environmental consultants at a public meeting, who made it fairly clear that they regarded volunteer data as charming but essentially worthless. They were, I noticed, rather quieter once the official results came in.

sections.label: D
sections.text: Tomasz, wild bee monitoring. I spent thirty years as an industrial chemist, and if you had told me then that amateurs could produce useful data, I would have smiled politely and changed the subject. In my world, measurement was something done by trained people with calibrated instruments. I signed up for the bee survey largely out of curiosity, having planted a meadow in what used to be my lawn, and I have had to eat a certain amount of humble pie. What no funded study can match is the sheer number of observers and the years they keep at it, and that turns out to compensate for a great deal of individual imprecision. I will admit that the protocol is rigid to the point of tedium: the same fifteen-minute window, the same route, the same form, whatever the weather. I grumble, but I understand that consistency is the whole point. My one real complaint is that the organizers seldom tell us what our observations have actually shown.

reading7.title: Away from the Desk: five professionals on remote work

sections.label: A
sections.text: Lena, architect. When our practice sent everyone home, my productivity went up, at least by the measures we usually use. I finished drawings faster and wasted far less time in traffic. What I had not appreciated was how many of my best ideas had come from overhearing other people's problems: a colleague swearing at a staircase that would not fit, a conversation by the coffee machine about a client's odd request. Those accidental exchanges simply disappeared, and the work became efficient but oddly flat. I now go into the office one day a week purely to be interrupted. The other lasting change has been in the way I communicate. When you cannot lean over someone's shoulder and point, you learn to write instructions that leave no room for misunderstanding, and my emails, I am told, have become almost alarmingly exact.

sections.label: B
sections.text: Kofi, translator. I have worked from home for nearly twenty years, so watching the rest of the world discover it has been, I confess, mildly entertaining. People ring me to describe, as though it were a new scientific finding, the experience of answering a work message at eleven at night in their pyjamas. I tell them what I learned the hard way in my first year: if the office is everywhere, work is everywhere too. My solution is slightly absurd but effective. Every morning I leave the house, walk once around the block and come back in through the front door as though arriving at work, and every evening I do the same in reverse. My children found this hilarious for years. I notice that several of their friends' parents now do something very similar.

sections.label: C
sections.text: Isabelle, team manager. My first months managing a team I could not see were uncomfortable, and I am not proud of how I handled them. I realized that I had been judging people, without quite admitting it, by how busy they looked: who arrived early, who stayed late, who always seemed to be on the phone. Remotely, none of that was visible, and I was forced to look instead at what people actually produced. The results surprised me. Some of my most visible employees turned out to be among the least effective, and one quiet analyst I had barely noticed was doing the work of two. I think the new approach is fairer. My concern is for the trainees who have joined us since, who learn mainly from watching others work and now have very little to watch.

sections.label: D
sections.text: Hamid, data analyst. I joined my company straight out of university, three weeks before the offices closed, and I have spent most of my career so far in my bedroom. My colleagues are friendly and they always tell me to get in touch whenever I need anything, but there is a world of difference between turning to the person at the next desk and scheduling a video call to ask what may well be a stupid question. More often than not, I spend an hour working it out alone rather than bother anyone. I have learned a lot that way, but slowly. Next month, at my annual review, I am going to ask whether I can spend at least three days a week in the office. Most of the senior people prefer to stay at home, so I may be fairly lonely there, but I suspect even proximity to a few of them would help.

sections.label: E
sections.text: Nora, customer service lead. We are a small company, and when our lease came up for renewal we decided not to renew it at all. The money we had been spending on rent now pays for better equipment for everyone and a training budget that we could never previously afford. Twice a year we hire a hall and spend two days together, which has turned out to be enough to keep a sense of belonging without the expense of permanent premises. The less obvious benefit has been in hiring. We used to recruit only from within commuting distance of the city centre. Now our team includes a former nurse from a fishing village, a parent who can only work school hours and a man who uses a wheelchair and found the old office almost impossible to reach. They are among the best people we have.

reading7.title: Keeping Time: four reviews of a new history of the clock

sections.label: A
sections.text: Reviewer A. Miriam Castellane's study of how standardized time reshaped daily life is, for the most part, a delight. She has a rare gift for making technical material painless: her account of how a pendulum regulates a clock is the clearest I have ever read, and she explains the problem of coordinating distant railway stations so lucidly that the reader feels, briefly, capable of solving it. The narrative moves briskly from monastery bells to factory whistles, and the anecdotes are well chosen. My reservation concerns the closing section on the digital age, which runs to well over a hundred pages and repeats points made far more economically earlier on; Castellane could have halved it without loss. Specialists may wish for more footnotes and fewer anecdotes, but that is not really the point. This is a book for the curious general reader, and such readers will be very well served.

sections.label: B
sections.text: Reviewer B. As a historian of the period, I opened Keeping Time with high hopes, and closed it with mixed feelings. Castellane's central argument, that the clock disciplined workers before it disciplined anyone else, has been made many times before, and she does little to sharpen or extend it. Where she excels is in the archive. Her use of the diaries, letters and household notebooks of ordinary people, a laundress, a signalman, a schoolgirl counting the minutes until the end of lessons, brings the abstract history of measurement vividly to life, and these passages alone justify the book. It is a pity, then, that her gaze rarely strays beyond Western Europe and North America. Other cultures had sophisticated and very different ways of dividing the day, and their near-total absence makes the book's subtitle, with its promise of a history of how humanity learned to keep time, look rather overconfident.

sections.label: C
sections.text: Reviewer C. There is much to admire in Keeping Time, not least the chapter on the railways, which is as gripping as a good thriller. I am less persuaded by the book's underlying mood. Castellane writes about the world before standardized time with unmistakable longing, as though medieval peasants spent their days in harmonious communion with the seasons, rather than labouring from dawn to dusk at the mercy of the weather. This rosy view distorts her conclusions: what she presents as a story of loss was, for many people, also one of gain. And yet I must concede that the book has got under my skin. Since reading it, I have caught myself glancing at my watch with a new self-consciousness, and I have twice left it on the kitchen table, deliberately, for an entire weekend.

sections.label: D
sections.text: Reviewer D. Few authors would dare to take on a subject this vast, and fewer still would emerge with their dignity intact. Castellane ranges with assurance from astronomy to labour history, from the engineering of watch springs to the psychology of punctuality, and the sheer breadth of the enterprise is part of its appeal. The book's most stimulating pages come at the very end, where she asks what happens to a society whose clocks are now synchronized invisibly, to a fraction of a second, by networks nobody sees. It is a pity that the illustrations, which include some fascinating early timetables, have been so poorly reproduced; many are too dark or too small to read, a lapse for which the publisher, not the author, must surely take responsibility.

listening.title: A documentary about the deep ocean

lines.en: Did you end up watching that documentary about the deep ocean? The one with the little submersible?

I did, last night. I'd expected to be bored, honestly. Those programs usually spend forty minutes on dramatic music and slow-motion explosions of plankton and about five on actual science. But this one was different. They let the footage speak for itself. There was a stretch of almost ten minutes with no narration at all, just the lights of the submersible drifting past creatures that looked as if they'd been designed by a committee of children.
Ten minutes of silence? That sounds like a good way to lose half your audience.

It would have been, in less confident hands. What struck me, though, was how candid the scientists were. One of them admitted that they'd spent three weeks at sea and found almost nothing they'd gone looking for. They'd planned to study a particular kind of coral, and the site turned out to be a field of mud.
So what did they do?

Improvised, more or less. They turned the cameras on whatever happened to swim by, and that's how they ended up filming an octopus nobody had ever recorded before. I found that rather heartening. We're always told that science is about careful planning, and it is, but half the good stuff seems to come out of what goes wrong.
You make it sound almost cheerful.

Well, not entirely. The last part was about companies that want to mine the seabed for metals, and the presenters were clearly worried. I don't think they were exaggerating. But it felt tacked on. A subject that serious deserved a film of its own, not a hurried few minutes at the very end.

lines.en: So, have you read the memo? Starting in the spring, we're trying out a four-day week for six months.
I have. I'm in two minds about it, to be honest. On paper it's wonderful. Who's going to object to a three-day weekend?
But?

But I've seen the targets, and they haven't reduced them at all. So it's the same workload squeezed into four days instead of five. I can already picture what Thursday evenings are going to look like.

I think you're being a bit gloomy. The whole point, as I understand it, is that we spend an absurd amount of time in meetings that achieve nothing. If they cut those, four days might genuinely be enough.
If. Has anyone actually said they're cutting meetings?

Not in so many words. Fair point. What persuaded me, though, was the part about the evaluation. They're not just going to ask whether we liked it. They're measuring output, sick days, the lot, and they've promised to share the results with everyone, whatever they show.
Well, that's more than they did with the open-plan office.
Exactly. Nobody ever told us how that turned out.
Nobody needed to. We were all sitting in it.
Quite. Anyway, I'm going to give it a fair chance. Six months isn't forever.
No, I suppose not. And if it's a disaster, at least it'll be a short one.

listening.title: Saving sounds: a talk by a sound recordist

lines.en: Good evening, everyone. I've been asked to talk about my work as a sound recordist, and I'd like to start with a confession. When I began, nearly twenty years ago, I wasn't interested in nature at all. I recorded trains. Old ones, mostly, on heritage railways, because I loved the rhythm of the wheels over the joints in the track. It was only when one of those lines closed for good that I realized what I had really been doing all along: not collecting sounds, but saving them.

That idea, that sounds can disappear, is at the heart of what I do now. We're used to the idea that landscapes change, that forests are cleared and rivers redirected. We're much less aware that soundscapes change too, often before anything visible happens. One of the marshes I've recorded every spring for twelve years still looks exactly as it did. But the chorus of frogs that used to fill it at dusk has thinned, and two of the species I once recorded there have fallen silent. If you only looked, you'd notice nothing at all.

People often ask me what equipment they need to get started, and I always disappoint them. The honest answer is that the most important tool is patience, and the second most important is a willingness to be cold. Most of my best recordings were made in the hour before dawn, after waiting in one spot for a very long time, and the microphone was the least remarkable thing about them.

The hardest part of the job, though, isn't the waiting. It's the noise. Not the noise of nature, but ours. There's almost nowhere left, even in remote parks, where you can record for fifteen minutes without hearing an aircraft, a road or a distant engine. When I started, I used to edit those sounds out. I don't anymore. I've come to think that a recording that pretends we aren't there is a kind of lie. Future listeners deserve to know what the world actually sounded like, intrusions and all.

Finally, a word about why any of this matters. Recordings like mine are increasingly used by researchers, who can assess the health of an ecosystem from the richness of its sounds, rather as a doctor listens to a heartbeat. But I'd be lying if I said that was why I do it. I do it because, every so often, I play a recording from fifteen years ago to a group of schoolchildren, and they ask me where they can go to hear that, and I have to tell them that I'm not sure they can.

the closure of a railway she had recorded

the pleasure she takes in teaching children
a wish to preserve sounds the next generation may never hear
the chance to spend long periods in remote places

listening.title: When cold was a harvest: a museum guide's talk

lines.en: Thanks for coming along this afternoon. Behind me is the icehouse, and before we go inside, I want you to imagine something: a world in which cold was a harvest. For most of the nineteenth century, and well into the twentieth in many rural areas, if you wanted to keep food cold in summer, you relied on ice that had been cut from a lake the previous winter.

The harvest usually began once the ice was thick enough to bear the weight of horses, which, on this lake, meant some time in January. Crews would first clear away the snow, then mark out a grid on the surface and cut along the lines, at first with long hand saws and later with horse-drawn cutters. The blocks were then floated along a channel of open water to the shore, which, when you think about it, is a wonderfully efficient way of letting the lake do the carrying.

People are often surprised to learn that the ice could last until the following autumn. The secret is in the walls you're about to see. They're double, and the gap between them is packed with sawdust, which was cheap and plentiful thanks to the local mills. Sawdust was also packed between the blocks themselves. Some of the ice melted, of course, but far less than you'd expect.

Now, it would be easy to romanticize all this, and visitors often do. It was hard, cold and genuinely dangerous work. Men fell through the ice, horses were lost, and the hours were brutal. I always mention that, not to spoil anyone's afternoon, but because the people who did this work deserve to be remembered as they were, and not as figures in a pretty winter scene on a calendar.

What intrigues me most, though, is how far the ice travelled. In the nineteenth century, ice cut from lakes in New England was shipped as far as the Caribbean and even India, packed in sawdust in the holds of sailing ships. Plenty of people at the time thought the whole idea was ridiculous. Who would pay to have frozen water carried halfway around the world? Quite a lot of people, as it turned out.

The trade disappeared, eventually, with the arrival of mechanical refrigeration, and most icehouses were demolished or simply left to collapse. This one survived largely because a local family used it for decades to store their boat. So, when we go in, do mind the step, and do notice the smell. All these years later, the walls still smell faintly of pine.

questions.q: According to the guide, the harvest began
choices: as soon as the lake had frozen over.
after the first heavy snowfall.
once the local mills had closed for the winter.
when the ice could support the weight of horses.
questions.explain: La récolte commençait « once the ice was thick enough to bear the weight of horses », en janvier sur ce lac.

choices: The lake itself provided the means of transport.
It meant that no horses were needed.
It reduced the amount of ice that melted.
It allowed the blocks to be cut more quickly.
questions.explain: Faire flotter les blocs dans un chenal, c'est « letting the lake do the carrying » : l'eau sert de moyen de transport.
