choices: the depth at which it was stored
insulation made from a cheap local material
the unusual thickness of the blocks
the cool summers in the region
questions.explain: Les murs doubles et les blocs étaient garnis de sciure, bon marché grâce aux scieries locales.

questions.q: Why does the guide mention the dangers of the work?
choices: to explain why the ice trade came to an end
to warn visitors against walking on frozen lakes
to correct a sentimental view of the past
to explain why few icehouses have survived
questions.explain: Il refuse de « romanticize » : les travailleurs méritent qu'on se souvienne d'eux tels qu'ils étaient, pas comme une jolie scène de calendrier.

questions.q: What does the guide say about the international ice trade?
choices: It was largely organized from this lake.
It succeeded despite early doubts about the idea.
It was abandoned because too much ice melted at sea.
It rarely made a profit for the shippers.
questions.explain: Beaucoup trouvaient l'idée ridicule, mais « quite a lot of people » ont payé pour cette glace : le commerce a réussi malgré le scepticisme.

questions.q: Why has this particular icehouse survived?
choices: It was protected by law.
Its walls were unusually strong.
It was put to a different use.
It was restored by the museum.
questions.explain: Une famille s'en servait pour ranger son bateau : le bâtiment a survécu grâce à ce nouvel usage.

listening.title: In defence of forgetting: a radio interview

lines.en: My guest today is the neuroscientist Ruth Adeyemi, whose new book argues that forgetting is not a failure of memory but one of its most important functions. Ruth, that sounds deliberately provocative.

It's meant to be a little provocative, yes, but I'd say it's less radical than it sounds. For a long time, researchers tended to treat forgetting as a kind of leak, information draining away because the system wasn't good enough to hold on to it. What's changed in recent decades is that there's growing evidence that the brain actively removes some memories. It spends energy doing it. And living things don't usually spend energy on something unless it's doing a job.
What job, though? Most of us would quite like to remember more, not less.

Would you, though? Imagine remembering every single time you'd ever parked your car, every one in perfect detail. Finding it today would be a nightmare, because all those old memories would be competing with the new one. Forgetting clears away the clutter, so that what's relevant now can stand out. It also lets us generalize. If you remembered every dog you'd ever met as a completely separate individual, you'd struggle to form the idea of a dog at all.
There are people, aren't there, who remember almost everything?

There are a small number of documented cases of people with extraordinary memory for their own lives, yes. And what's striking is that several of them describe it as much as a burden as a gift. They can't let go of embarrassments or quarrels the way the rest of us do. I'm careful not to draw sweeping conclusions from a handful of people, but it does suggest that a perfect memory might not be the blessing we imagine.
Your book also has a chapter on what you call productive forgetting in everyday life. That sounds suspiciously like an excuse for losing one's keys.

My own family has accused me of exactly that. No, the point is more modest. A lot of people are frightened that ordinary forgetfulness is the first sign of something serious. And of course, if someone's memory is changing noticeably, they should talk to their doctor. But walking into a room and forgetting why you came in is not, in itself, a cause for alarm. Usually it just means your brain has decided, quite sensibly, that something else matters more.
Is there anything listeners can do to forget better, so to speak?

I'd put it the other way round. If you want to remember what matters, stop trying to remember everything. People photograph every meal and record every lecture, and then never look at any of it, and there's some evidence that handing an experience over to a device can make us less likely to remember it ourselves. Choose what matters, give it your full attention, and let the rest go. That isn't laziness. It's how memory seems to be designed to work.

questions.q: How does Ruth respond to the suggestion that her argument is provocative?
choices: She admits she exaggerated it to attract readers.
She says it is less extreme than it may first appear.
She says most researchers have rejected it.
questions.explain: « Less radical than it sounds » : elle reconnaît un peu de provocation mais relativise la nouveauté de sa thèse.

questions.q: Why does Ruth mention that the brain spends energy on forgetting?
choices: to show that forgetting is an active process with a purpose
to explain why tired people forget more easily
to suggest that memory is an inefficient system
questions.explain: Un organisme ne dépense pas d'énergie pour rien : si le cerveau efface activement, c'est que l'oubli a une fonction.

questions.q: The example of the parked car illustrates
choices: how easily people lose track of objects.
why detailed memories fade so quickly.
how old memories could interfere with recent ones.
questions.explain: Si l'on se souvenait de chaque stationnement, les anciens souvenirs « would be competing with the new one ».

questions.q: What does Ruth say about people with exceptional memory?
choices: Their experience suggests total recall has drawbacks.
They prove that memory can be trained.
They are usually unaware of their unusual ability.
questions.explain: Plusieurs décrivent leur mémoire comme un fardeau, car ils n'oublient ni les gênes ni les disputes ; elle reste prudente mais y voit un indice.

questions.q: What is Ruth's attitude to ordinary forgetfulness?
choices: It should always be checked by a doctor.
It is generally no cause for concern.
It is mainly a result of stress.
questions.explain: Oublier pourquoi on est entré dans une pièce « is not, in itself, a cause for alarm » ; le médecin n'est conseillé qu'en cas de changement notable.

questions.q: What advice does Ruth give listeners?
choices: Record important events so that you can review them.
Practise memory exercises regularly.
Be selective about what you pay attention to.
questions.explain: « Choose what matters, give it your full attention, and let the rest go » ; elle critique au contraire le fait de tout photographier ou enregistrer.

listening.title: Translating play: an interview with a game translator

lines.en: I'm joined today by Mateo Ferreira, who translates video games, a job I suspect many of our listeners didn't know existed. Mateo, how did you end up doing this?

Entirely by accident. I trained as a literary translator, and I was working on a rather serious novel when a friend asked whether I could help with a game his studio was making. I said yes mainly because the novel was going badly and I wanted an excuse to escape it for a while. I assumed it would be a few weeks of translating menu labels. It turned out to be about two hundred thousand words of dialogue, a lot of it jokes.
Jokes must be the hardest part.

Everyone assumes so, and they're partly right. A pun almost never survives the journey from one language to another. But the real challenge isn't the joke itself. It's that the player has to laugh at the same moment, because the whole scene has been built around that laugh. So I'm not translating the joke so much as replacing it with something that does the same job at the same time. Sometimes the new joke has nothing whatsoever to do with the original.
Doesn't that bother the writers?

Some of them, at first. I've learned to explain what I'm going to do before I do it, rather than afterwards. Once most writers understand that I'm protecting the experience rather than vandalizing their text, they become remarkably generous. One even told me he preferred my version of a scene to his own. I didn't believe him for a second, but it was kind of him to say so.
What about the technical side? I imagine there are constraints that a translator of novels never faces.

Constantly. The words have to fit in a box on the screen, and French or German can easily run a third longer than English. A character's line might have to fit into the time it takes them to open a door. And very often I'm translating without seeing the game at all, just lines in a spreadsheet, out of order. I might get a line saying, watch out, it's right behind you, with no idea what it is. You learn to ask a great many questions.
Do you still translate literature?

Now and then. And I'd say the games have made me a better literary translator, not a worse one. They cured me of a kind of reverence. I used to cling to every word of the original as if it were sacred. Now I ask what a sentence is for, what it's trying to do to the reader, and I'm far more willing to be bold to achieve that. Some of my colleagues think that's dangerous. I think it's the job.

questions.q: Why did Mateo first agree to translate a game?
choices: He was struggling with another project.
He wanted to learn more about technology.
He was offered an unusually large fee.
questions.explain: Il a dit oui « mainly because the novel was going badly » : il voulait s'échapper de ce roman.

questions.q: According to Mateo, the real difficulty with jokes is
choices: finding puns that work in both languages.
making sure the player laughs at the intended moment.
persuading writers to accept his changes.
questions.explain: La difficulté n'est pas la blague elle-même mais le moment du rire, autour duquel la scène est construite.

questions.q: How has Mateo learned to work with the writers?
choices: by keeping as close as possible to their text
by letting them choose between several versions
by explaining his approach before he starts
questions.explain: « I've learned to explain what I'm going to do before I do it, rather than afterwards ».

questions.q: What does Mateo suggest about the writer who preferred his version?
choices: The comment was probably kindness rather than a sincere judgment.
The comment confirmed that his approach was right.
The comment embarrassed him in front of the team.
questions.explain: « I didn't believe him for a second, but it was kind » : il y voit de la gentillesse, pas un vrai jugement.

questions.q: What problem does he mention about translating from spreadsheets?
choices: The files are often incomplete.
He frequently lacks the context of a line.
He has to cut every line by a third.
questions.explain: Les répliques arrivent dans le désordre, sans le jeu : il ne sait pas ce que désigne « it » dans « it's right behind you ».

questions.q: How has translating games affected his literary work?
choices: It has made him more careful with every word.
It has caused disagreements with his publishers.
It has made him readier to depart from the literal text.
questions.explain: Il ne s'accroche plus à chaque mot comme s'il était sacré et accepte d'être audacieux pour produire le même effet sur le lecteur.

listening.title: Starting over: five people on changing career

lines.en: I'd been in banking for nearly fifteen years when the company offered unpaid leave to anyone who wanted it. Money was tight across the industry, and I suppose they were hoping to save a few salaries. I took three months, mostly intending to travel, but a friend talked me into helping with a reading program at her children's school. Twice a week I sat in a corridor with an eight-year-old and a picture book. By the end of the first month, I knew I wasn't going back. My family thought I'd lost my mind, frankly, and some of them still do. But I've never been so tired or so certain.

Everyone warned me I'd miss the intellectual side of engineering, the problem-solving, and I was braced for that. It hasn't happened. Designing a garden for a steep, shady plot with heavy clay soil and a client who insists on roses is as hard a problem as anything I faced at the firm. What I hadn't prepared for was the money. I'd done the sums and I'd saved, but there's a world of difference between knowing your income will halve and actually living on half. That first winter was genuinely frightening. It's better now, but I still check my bank balance more often than is healthy.

When I left journalism to train as a nurse, I assumed I was starting from scratch. I'd forgotten all the biology I'd ever learned, which admittedly wasn't much, and the first term was a struggle. What took me completely by surprise was how much of my old job I'd brought with me. Patients are frightened, and they don't always tell you the important thing first. Twenty years of interviewing people had taught me to listen for what isn't being said, and to ask the second question rather than settling for the first answer. My supervisors noticed it long before I did.

People assume I left the restaurant because of the stress, and kitchens certainly are stressful, but I actually loved that part. I'm one of those people who work best with a dozen orders coming in at once. What I couldn't live with any longer was the timetable. My daughter was starting school, and I worked every evening and every weekend, which meant I saw her for about an hour a day, usually over breakfast while I was half asleep. Software development came about because I'd always tinkered with computers. It's less exciting, I'll admit. But I'm home by six.

I'd love to tell you I walked out of my office one day and never looked back, but that isn't what happened, and I wouldn't recommend it. For two years I worked four days a week at a software company and spent the fifth, plus most weekends, at the pottery studio. It was exhausting, and there were times I resented both jobs. But it meant that when I finally left, I already had customers, a small reputation and a realistic idea of what I would earn. I meet people now who've thrown everything in for a dream. Some of them are doing brilliantly. More of them, sadly, are not.

questions.q: What made Speaker one decide to change career?
choices: pressure from family members
an experience during a break from work
the loss of a job in a difficult industry
a long-held ambition to teach
questions.explain: Pendant un congé sans solde de trois mois, le bénévolat en lecture à l'école l'a convaincu ; la famille, elle, trouvait l'idée folle.

questions.q: What has Speaker two found hardest about the change?
choices: missing the intellectual challenge of the old job
learning the practical skills of gardening
adjusting to a much lower income
dealing with demanding clients
questions.explain: « What I hadn't prepared for was the money » : vivre avec la moitié du revenu a été effrayant ; le défi intellectuel, lui, ne manque pas.

questions.q: What surprised Speaker three after changing career?
choices: how quickly the biology came back
how frightened most patients are
how strict the supervisors were
how useful the skills from the previous job proved
questions.explain: Vingt ans d'interviews lui ont appris à écouter ce qui n'est pas dit : ses anciennes compétences se sont révélées précieuses.

questions.q: Why did Speaker four change career?
choices: to be more available for family life
to escape a stressful working environment
to earn a higher salary
after being offered a job by a friend
questions.explain: Le problème était l'horaire : voir sa fille une heure par jour ; le stress, au contraire, lui plaisait.

questions.q: What does Speaker five suggest about changing career?
choices: It is best to make a clean break.
The new career should be related to the old one.
It is wiser to make the transition gradually.
The financial risks are usually exaggerated.
questions.explain: Deux ans à quatre jours par semaine avant de partir : clientèle et réputation étaient prêtes ; il déconseille de tout quitter d'un coup.

listening.title: A month offline: five people on giving up social media

lines.en: I'd never have tried it on my own initiative. My son, who's fifteen, accused me over dinner of being worse with my phone than he was, which was outrageous and also, as it turned out, true. He bet me I couldn't last a month without any social media at all. The stakes were doing the dishes for the following month. I deleted the apps that night, mainly out of pride. I'll be honest, the first week was humiliating. I kept picking up the phone and staring at a screen with nothing on it, like someone opening the fridge for the fifth time in the hope that something new has appeared.

I'd expected to miss the news, or the endless photographs of other people's vacations, and I didn't miss those in the slightest. What I hadn't foreseen was how much of my social life had quietly moved into group chats. Plans were made there. Birthdays were organized there. Twice I found out about a get-together only afterwards, when somebody said how sorry they were that I couldn't make it. Nobody had meant to leave me out. It simply hadn't occurred to anyone that a message might not reach me. That was the part that stung, far more than anything I'd prepared myself to give up.

The change came in the second week, and it caught me off guard. I picked up a novel one evening, a long one I'd started and abandoned twice, and when I next looked at the clock, two hours had gone by. I hadn't read like that since I was a student. I'd assumed that my attention span had simply worn out with age, the way knees do. It hadn't. It had been chopped into little pieces, a few seconds at a time, and given a month off, it grew back. I find that both encouraging and slightly alarming.

When the month ended, I didn't feel any great urge to go back, but I didn't feel virtuous enough to stay away either. So I compromised. I reinstalled one app, the one I use to keep in touch with relatives overseas, and left the others off my phone. I check them on the computer once a day, at a fixed time, sitting down, as if I were reading the paper. It sounds terribly regimented, and my friends tease me about it. But I've found that when it's a deliberate choice rather than a reflex, I actually enjoy it more.

I did the month because my whole office was doing it, and I'll admit I found the exercise rather self-congratulatory. Afterwards, everyone posted online about how much calmer they felt, and the irony was lost on no one. My real objection, though, is that it puts all the responsibility on the individual. My phone isn't constantly buzzing because I'm weak-willed. It's buzzing because my manager sends messages at ten at night and expects a reply by morning. You can delete every app you like, but until that changes, nothing much will.

questions.q: Why did Speaker one give up social media?
choices: in response to a challenge from a family member
on the advice of a doctor
because a colleague had recommended it
after reading about the benefits online
questions.explain: Son fils de quinze ans lui a lancé un pari ; il a supprimé les applications « mainly out of pride ».

questions.q: What did Speaker two find most difficult?
choices: being cut off from current events
resisting the urge to check the phone
explaining the experiment to friends
being left out of social arrangements
questions.explain: Les sorties s'organisaient dans les discussions de groupe ; découvrir après coup deux rencontres manquées « stung » ; les nouvelles ne lui ont pas manqué.

questions.q: What benefit did Speaker three discover?
choices: more time to spend with friends
a renewed capacity for sustained concentration
a better night's sleep
a new interest in writing
questions.explain: Deux heures de lecture sans voir le temps passer : sa capacité d'attention, morcelée, « grew back ».

questions.q: How did Speaker four respond once the month was over?
choices: by giving up social media for good
by going straight back to old habits
by resuming use in a more controlled way
by persuading friends to try the experiment
questions.explain: Une seule application réinstallée, les autres consultées une fois par jour à heure fixe : un retour encadré et délibéré.

questions.q: What is Speaker five's main criticism of the experiment?
choices: It was too short to make any real difference.
It ignored pressures that come from the workplace.
It was imposed on staff against their wishes.
It failed to make anyone feel calmer.
questions.explain: Le téléphone vibre parce que son patron écrit à vingt-deux heures : rien ne changera tant que ces attentes au travail resteront.

writing.title: Car-free city centres
writing.prompt: Read the two texts below on the idea of banning cars from city centres. Write an essay in which you summarize and evaluate the main points made in both texts. Express the ideas in your own words as far as possible and include your own views on the issue. Write 240-280 words.
texts: For most of the last century, city centres were redesigned around the private car, and we are still living with the consequences: congestion, noise and air that damages our health. Cities that have closed their central districts to traffic have frequently found that the predicted collapse of trade never materializes. On the contrary, pedestrians linger, browse and come back, and shops that once complained loudly about lost parking often end up busier than before. Streets freed from cars can be given back to people, with trees, benches and space for children to play. The question is not whether we can afford to do this, but whether we can afford not to.

Banning cars from city centres has an undeniable appeal, particularly for those who live within walking distance of them. For many others, however, the car is not a luxury but a necessity. Elderly residents, people with disabilities and parents juggling work and childcare cannot always rely on public transport, which in many cities remains infrequent, overcrowded or simply absent after dark. A ban introduced before proper alternatives are in place risks turning the centre into a pleasant enclave for the fit and the fortunate. Reducing traffic is a worthy goal, but it should be pursued gradually, with investment in buses and trains coming first.

require.label: Au moins 4 paragraphes : introduction, texte 1, texte 2, ton avis
Au moins 6 connecteurs logiques variés (however, whereas, since, therefore…)
Au moins 2 expressions d'évaluation ou de nuance (arguably, nevertheless, in my view…)

writing.model:
Few urban debates generate as much heat as the question of whether cars should be banished from city centres. Both texts acknowledge the harm done by traffic, yet they differ sharply on how quickly, and at whose expense, it should be reduced.

The first writer makes a forceful case for closing central districts to vehicles. Not only would residents breathe cleaner air and enjoy quieter streets, but local businesses, contrary to their fears, frequently prosper once shoppers are able to stroll at leisure. Although this argument is persuasive, it arguably rests on the experience of cities that already enjoy excellent public transport, and it says little about those for whom walking is not a realistic option.

This is precisely the gap the second text addresses. Its author contends that an outright ban would penalize the elderly, people with disabilities and busy parents, who depend on their cars because buses and trains are often unreliable. Consequently, a car-free centre could become an attractive playground for the privileged. I find this objection compelling; nevertheless, the insistence that transport must improve first could easily become an excuse for indefinite delay, since governments rarely invest in alternatives without pressure.

In my view, therefore, the most sensible approach combines the ambition of the first text with the caution of the second. Cities should set a firm date for restricting traffic while using the intervening period to expand public transport and guarantee access for those with genuine needs. In this way, the benefits of quieter streets would be shared by everyone rather than enjoyed by a fortunate few.

writing.title: The arts at school
writing.prompt: Read the two texts below on the place of the arts in the school timetable. Write an essay in which you summarize and evaluate the main points made in both texts. Express the ideas in your own words as far as possible and include your own views on the issue. Write 240-280 words.
texts: Schools have a duty to prepare young people for the world they will actually live in, and that world is increasingly shaped by science and technology. Employers report persistent shortages of engineers, programmers and technicians, while graduates in many other fields struggle to find work that matches their qualifications. With timetables already overcrowded, something has to give. Reducing compulsory hours in music, drama and art would free up time for the mathematics and science that open doors. Students who are passionate about the arts could still pursue them through clubs and optional courses; what we cannot do is leave the majority unprepared for a technical economy.

It is tempting to treat art, music and drama as pleasant extras that can be trimmed whenever time is short. Yet the arts teach things that no other subject teaches as well: how to tolerate uncertainty, how to revise one's work in response to criticism, and how to collaborate on something that has no single correct answer. These are precisely the capacities that employers say they value most. Moreover, for many students the arts are what make school bearable, the one lesson in which they genuinely succeed. Cutting them may produce better test scores in the short term, but at a lasting cost to engagement and creativity.

require.label: Au moins 4 paragraphes : introduction, texte 1, texte 2, ton avis
Au moins 6 connecteurs logiques variés (however, whereas, since, therefore…)
Au moins 2 expressions d'évaluation ou de nuance (arguably, nevertheless, in my view…)

writing.model:
Whether schools should sacrifice time spent on the arts in order to strengthen science and technology is a question that sets economic realism against a broader vision of education. The two texts take opposing positions, although each concedes more to the other than might first appear.

The first writer argues that education must reflect the demands of the job market, which currently favours technical skills. Since timetables are already full, the author proposes cutting compulsory arts lessons and offering them as optional activities instead. This argument has the merit of honesty; however, it assumes that the worth of a subject can be measured by its direct link to employment, which strikes me as a rather narrow definition of what schools are for.

The second text, by contrast, maintains that creative subjects develop qualities such as resilience, openness to criticism and the ability to work with others on open-ended problems. Interestingly, these are the very skills employers claim to want, so the argument partly turns the first writer's economic logic against itself. The point about motivation is also important, because a student who flourishes in drama may be more willing to persevere in mathematics.

On balance, I find the second position more convincing. Admittedly, schools cannot teach everything, and some reorganization of the timetable may be unavoidable. Nevertheless, reducing the arts to an optional extra would mainly penalize students whose families cannot pay for private lessons. A better solution would be to bring creative approaches into scientific subjects, so that young people are never forced to choose between imagination and technical competence.

writing.title: Is space exploration worth the cost?
writing.prompt: Read the two texts below on public spending on space exploration. Write an essay in which you summarize and evaluate the main points made in both texts. Express the ideas in your own words as far as possible and include your own views on the issue. Write 240-280 words.
texts: Critics of space exploration often ask why we spend money on distant planets when there are problems to solve at home. The question misunderstands how progress works. Technologies developed for space missions have found their way into everyday life, and satellites now allow us to forecast storms and to monitor deforestation and melting ice. Just as importantly, space exploration inspires. Countless scientists trace their vocation to a childhood spent watching rocket launches. A society that stops looking beyond its own horizon may discover that it has also stopped imagining solutions to the difficulties closer to home.

There is no denying that rockets are thrilling, but thrills are an expensive basis for public policy. The sums devoted to sending people beyond our atmosphere could instead fund research into renewable energy, clean water or diseases that still affect millions. Supporters of space programs point to useful inventions that emerged along the way, yet many of those discoveries could surely have been made more cheaply through direct investment. Moreover, the dream of escaping to another world risks encouraging complacency about this one. Until we have learned to look after the only planet known to support life, ambitious missions elsewhere look less like progress than distraction.

Au moins 6 connecteurs logiques variés (however, whereas, since, therefore…)
Au moins 2 expressions d'évaluation ou de nuance (arguably, nevertheless, in my view…)

writing.model:
Few public expenditures are as visible, or as controversial, as the money spent on exploring space. The two texts disagree fundamentally about whether such spending is an investment in the future or a costly diversion from urgent problems on Earth.

The first writer contends that space programs repay their cost in two ways. On a practical level, they generate technologies that benefit everyday life, notably the satellites we rely on to track storms and environmental damage; on a less tangible level, they inspire young people to pursue careers in science. While the second claim is difficult to measure, I find it plausible, since ambitious projects capture the imagination in a way that routine research rarely does.

The second writer, however, regards this enthusiasm as an unaffordable luxury. From this perspective, the same resources would achieve more if directed at pressing needs such as clean energy and public health, and the useful by-products of space research could have been obtained more efficiently by funding them directly. This argument is undeniably logical. Nevertheless, it underestimates how often major discoveries arise unexpectedly from work undertaken for quite different purposes, which is precisely why they cannot always be planned.

Ultimately, I am not persuaded that we face a simple choice between the stars and the Earth. Much of the data on which climate scientists depend is gathered from space, so the two goals are arguably complementary rather than competing. Consequently, the real question is not whether to explore space but how to ensure that exploration serves the needs of the planet we already inhabit.

writing.title: The place that changed my mind
writing.prompt: A travel magazine is running a series called “The place that changed my mind”. Write an article for the series describing a place you visited that challenged your expectations. Explain how and why your view changed, and what the experience taught you about travelling. Write 280-320 words.

Au moins 1 question rhétorique pour impliquer le lecteur
Au moins 5 connecteurs logiques ou temporels variés

writing.model:
The Island I Wanted to Avoid

Have you ever dreaded a trip so thoroughly that you almost cancelled it? That was precisely my state of mind on the ferry to a small island off the northern Pacific coast, where my cousin had insisted we spend a week. The forecast promised seven days of rain, and I spent the entire crossing composing complaints in my head.

The first morning seemed to confirm my worst fears. Fog swallowed the shoreline, the village consisted of a general store, a church and a café with unpredictable opening hours, and there was no phone signal. By lunchtime I had read the café menu four times and was seriously considering the next ferry home.

What changed my mind was a walk my cousin practically forced me to take. Within minutes of leaving the road, we were in a forest so dense and so green that it seemed to absorb sound itself. Moss hung from every branch like heavy curtains, enormous trees rose into the mist, and the only noise was the patient dripping of water and, occasionally, the throaty commentary of a raven. The rain, which I had regarded as an obstacle, turned out to be the whole point: without it, none of this extraordinary life could exist.

Over the following days, I stopped checking my phone and started noticing things instead: the way the tide rearranged the beach twice a day, the neighbours who waved at strangers, the simple pleasure of a hot drink after a soaking. Consequently, by the end of the week, I was the one who wanted to stay.

The lesson, I think, is that our expectations are often the least reliable item in our luggage. If we travel only in search of what we already know we like, we will rarely be surprised. Sometimes the best thing a destination can do is refuse to give us what we came for.

writing.title: Save our library
writing.prompt: Your local newspaper has reported that the town council plans to close the central public library and replace it with a smaller “digital hub” offering online services. Write a letter to the editor expressing your views on the proposal. Explain what the library means to the community and suggest alternatives that the council should consider. Write 280-320 words.

Au moins 6 connecteurs logiques formels (however, furthermore, consequently…)
Au moins 2 marqueurs de registre formel (furthermore, I would urge, consequently…)

writing.model:
Dear Editor,

I am writing in response to your recent report on the council's plan to close the central library and replace it with a so-called digital hub. While I appreciate the financial pressures facing the council, I believe this proposal fundamentally misunderstands what the library provides.

To describe the library simply as a building full of books is to overlook most of its value. On any weekday morning, it welcomes parents and toddlers at story time, retirees reading newspapers they could not otherwise afford and job seekers receiving help with applications. In the afternoon, it becomes a quiet place to study for teenagers who have nowhere else to work. Furthermore, it is one of the very few indoor spaces in our town where nobody is expected to spend money.

The proposed hub would undoubtedly offer useful online services. However, a row of computers cannot replace a librarian who notices that an elderly visitor is struggling, nor can it provide the sense of belonging that comes from a shared public space. Moreover, the residents who depend most on the library are precisely those least likely to benefit from a purely digital service.

I would therefore urge the council to explore alternatives before taking an irreversible step. Part of the building could be rented to community organizations or a café, generating income while keeping the library open. Opening hours could be adjusted rather than eliminated, and volunteers, many of whom have already offered their help, could support professional staff at busier times. Finally, the council might seek partnerships with local businesses willing to sponsor specific programs.

Once a library closes, it is rarely reopened. Consequently, I hope that councillors will listen to the many residents who rely on it and reconsider a decision that would leave our town considerably poorer in every sense but the financial one.

Sincerely,
Priya Sharma

writing.prompt: You are a member of the student council at your college. Last year, the college introduced a peer mentoring scheme in which senior students support students in their first year. The principal has asked you to write a report assessing how successful the scheme has been, identifying any problems and making recommendations for its future. Write 280-320 words.

Au moins 2 formulations de recommandation (I recommend, should, I would suggest…)
Au moins 5 connecteurs logiques (however, in addition, firstly, finally…)
Au moins 2 verbes au passif (was introduced, were assigned…)

writing.model:
Introduction
The aim of this report is to assess the peer mentoring scheme introduced at the start of last year, to identify its main weaknesses and to recommend improvements. It is based on a questionnaire completed by over two hundred first-year students and on interviews with twelve mentors.

Benefits of the scheme
Overall, the scheme has been well received. A clear majority of first-year respondents stated that their mentor had helped them settle in more quickly, particularly during the first few weeks, when timetables, deadlines and unfamiliar buildings can feel overwhelming. Several students commented that they found it easier to admit difficulties to an older student than to a teacher. Mentors, for their part, reported that the role had increased their confidence and given them experience worth mentioning in future applications.

Problems identified
However, the scheme has not worked equally well for everyone. Mentors were assigned at random, so some pairs had little in common and met only once or twice. In addition, mentors received a single short training session, and a number of them admitted feeling unprepared when students raised serious personal or academic concerns. Finally, interest declined noticeably after the first term, partly because meetings were never formally scheduled.

Recommendations
In light of these findings, I would make the following recommendations. Firstly, students should be matched according to shared courses or interests rather than randomly. Secondly, I recommend that mentors receive more thorough training, including clear guidance on when a problem should be referred to staff. Thirdly, a short monthly meeting should be built into the timetable, so that contact does not depend entirely on goodwill.

Conclusion
In conclusion, the scheme has clearly made the transition to college easier for many students and deserves to continue. Provided that the changes suggested above are implemented, it could become one of the most valuable features of student life here.

Write a review briefly describing the film, explaining how it changed your thinking and saying whether you would recommend it to others. Write 280-320 words.

writing.model:
After Dark: the documentary that made me look up

I have always regarded light pollution as a minor inconvenience, the sort of issue that concerns amateur astronomers and nobody else. After Dark, Léa Fontaine's quietly powerful documentary, persuaded me within an hour that I had been badly mistaken.

The film follows a year in the life of a small town that decides, after a heated public debate, to dim and redirect its street lighting. Rather than relying on a narrator, Fontaine lets the residents tell the story: a skeptical shop owner convinced that crime will soar, a retired nurse who has not seen the Milky Way since childhood, and a biologist who spends her nights counting moths. Their conversations are interspersed with breathtaking sequences of the night sky gradually reappearing above the rooftops.

What changed my thinking was not the beauty of those images, striking as they are, but the evidence quietly accumulated around them. I had no idea that artificial light could disorient migrating birds, disrupt insects that pollinate crops or interfere with our own sleep. The film presents these findings without hysteria, which makes them all the more disturbing. Equally memorable is the shop owner's gradual conversion: when crime fails to rise, he admits on camera that he had simply never thought of darkness as something worth having.

The documentary is not flawless. At almost two hours it is somewhat too long, and a section on the history of street lighting, while interesting, slows the momentum considerably. Moreover, viewers hoping for practical advice on what they can do themselves may feel slightly short-changed.

Nevertheless, I would recommend After Dark wholeheartedly, particularly to anyone who, like me, assumed that a dark night sky was a luxury rather than a necessity. You may never look at a street lamp in quite the same way again.

writing.title: Is ambition always a virtue?
writing.prompt: Your class has been discussing whether ambition is always a positive quality. Your teacher has asked you to write an essay considering the advantages and disadvantages of ambition, both for individuals and for society, and giving your own opinion. Write 280-320 words.

require.label: Au moins 5 paragraphes (introduction, pour, contre, nuance, conclusion)
Au moins 6 connecteurs logiques variés
Au moins 3 marqueurs d'argumentation nuancée (admittedly, whereas, on balance…)

writing.model:
Ambition is one of those qualities we are taught to admire from an early age. Parents praise it, schools reward it and entire industries are built around encouraging it. Yet a moment's reflection suggests that ambition is less straightforwardly admirable than its reputation implies, and that its value depends largely on what it is directed towards.

There is no denying that ambition has driven much of human progress. Without the desire to achieve something difficult, few scientists would endure years of failed experiments, and few artists would persevere through decades of obscurity. On an individual level, ambition gives shape to a life: it provides goals, motivates effort and can turn modest beginnings into remarkable achievements. Societies that discourage it, whether through rigid hierarchies or a habit of mocking those who try, arguably condemn themselves to stagnation.

Admittedly, ambition also has a darker side. When success is measured solely by status or wealth, the ambitious may come to treat colleagues as rivals and friends as stepping stones. Furthermore, relentless striving can be exhausting, and many high achievers describe a perpetual dissatisfaction, as though each goal reached merely revealed the next. In politics or business, unchecked ambition can lead people to cut corners, ignore risks or exploit others.

The crucial distinction, in my view, lies between ambition for oneself and ambition for something. A researcher determined to find a better treatment and a researcher determined to become famous may work equally hard, whereas only the first is likely to rejoice if a colleague finds the answer first. The former kind of ambition is generous; the latter is easily corrupted.

On balance, therefore, ambition is neither a virtue nor a vice in itself. It is a form of energy, and like all energy it can illuminate or burn. Rather than simply urging young people to be ambitious, we should help them reflect on what their ambition is for.
